articles.author: AXEC
articles.description:
An AI agent should never keep access simply because nobody remembered to remove it.
Access should begin with a specific job, not a broad role.
For a support-summary agent, the scope might be:
Read selected support records
Summarize recent conversations
Work for one hour
Access no export, delete, or modification functions
That definition gives the agent enough authority to complete the task without turning temporary work into permanent access.
A permission should have more than a name. It should have limits.
Set boundaries for:
Time: When does access expire?
Resources: Which records, systems, or folders can the agent reach?
Actions: Can it read, write, export, or approve?
Purpose: What task is the access meant to support?
The narrower the task, the easier it is to review and control.
Agent …
articles.title: The Dangerous Part of Agent Access Is What Happens After the Task

articles.author: AXEC
articles.description:
Copying a user's permissions into an AI agent is a security shortcut that creates authority nobody can clearly explain.
A person may be allowed to access many systems because of their role. An agent working on one task should not automatically receive the same reach.
The real question is not, “Who started this request?”
It is, “What is this agent allowed to do for this specific task?”
That distinction matters when an agent can call tools, access records, or trigger business actions without waiting for a person at every step.
Consider an agent helping a support team summarize customer feedback.
It may need to:
Read selected support records
Group recurring issues
Draft a summary for review
It should not automatically be able to:
Export the entire support database
Modify billing information
C…
articles.title: An AI Agent Should Not Inherit Your Entire Permission Set

articles.author: Janet Malone
articles.description:
When I started building a small browser tool for narrowing down home security cameras, the default architecture was a form that posted answers to a backend and returned recommendations. I didn't want that. The questions get personal fast: do you rent, is there a power outlet near the door, do you need night vision in a shared hallway, are you home during the day. Those answers can describe a home's layout and occupancy. Putting them in a request log felt like a bad trade for a free tool.
So the recommendation logic runs entirely in the browser. No signup, no email gate, no server-side session. I keep in-progress answers in sessionStorage rather than localStorage, which means they disappear when the tab closes. That's deliberate: I don't need a persistent profile of someone's security setup…
articles.title: Keeping a home security camera helper out of your request logs

articles.author: DapperX
articles.description:
Email automation usually fails in the least satisfying way: a test waits, times out, and prints message not found. The common response is to add another retry or increase the polling window.
That can help when delivery is genuinely slow. But it can also hide a wrong recipient, a stale inbox, a malformed test address, or a message that arrived with the wrong flow identifier. When every failure looks like a timeout, the team learns very little from the run.
In my own automation work, a small event receipt has been more useful than a larger retry budget. The receipt is a compact record of what the workflow asked for, what the mail system accepted, and what the test actually observed. It turns email from a mysterious side effect into a debuggable step.
A retry answers only one question: “Did t…
articles.title: Email Automation Needs a Receipt, Not a Retry

articles.description:
CVE-2026-15176: The alias Rewrite Overflow That Survived Since 2005


The oldest of the five NGINX flaws fixed in 1.30.6 and 1.31.7 is also the one with the widest version range. CVE-2026-15176 affects releases from 0.1.29 onward, which means it has been present in essentially every NGINX build shipped since May 2005. F5 rates it 9.2 Critical on CVSS v4.0, and F5's own engineers are credited with finding it.
The flaw lives in the gap between two phases of request handling. NGINX first selects a location, then, if that location contains a rewrite, it can change the request URI and start location selection again. During the interval after the rewrite and before the next location is chosen, the request still carries the old location's context.
If that old location used alias, and if anything …

I work a lot with the OpenTelemetry Collector in Kubernetes, and I reproduce problems like this in a throwaway AWS account before I write about them.
Here is how it works, and how to build it yourself.

Short answer


Trust without traceability is not trust—it’s assumption. In AI governance, regulatory compliance, and professional accountability, verifiable provenance of decisions, data, and model behavior is non-negotiable.
92% of enterprise AI adopters cite auditability as a top-three requirement for production deployment (IBM Institute for Business Value, 2023).

The EU AI Act (Art. 13) mandates “technical documentation” and “logging mechanisms” for high-risk systems—traceability is legally embedded.

Brazil’s Marco Legal da Inteligência Artificial (PL 2338/2023) requires traceable decision logic for public-sector AI applications.

IBM Granite models include built-in observability hooks for input/output logging, prompt versioning, and confidence scoring—enabling reproducible inference.…

articles.description:
If you already use Playwright for end-to-end tests, you have everything you need to check a page for broken links. The browser can collect every link after JavaScript has run, and Playwright's built-in API client can request each one without opening a new tab. This post builds a small, practical broken link test step by step, and covers the parts that usually go wrong: false positives, rate limits and redirects.
Open a page with page.goto().
Collect every href from <a> elements (and src from images, if you want).
Request each unique URL with Playwright's request fixture.
Fail the test if any of them return an error.
a.href in the browser returns an absolute URL, so relative links are resolved for you.
